title: Post-session knowledge check
notes: PROVISIONAL INSTRUMENT. Revised 2026-10-28 so every item tests real farming knowledge that the game and its feedback actually teach, in plain language for smallholder farmers. Still needs supervisor review before any study use. Editing this file is enough to change the instrument - no code changes are required. The post-test uses the same eight items as the pre-test, presented in a different order, so that the two scores are directly comparable.

questions.text: A dry season is expected and you have limited water. How much land should you plant?
options: The whole field - more land always means more harvest
Extra land, so that at least some of it survives
The same as last season, so nothing changes
Only as much as your water can carry through to harvest
questions.explanation: A crop that dries out before it matures gives nothing back, but it still used seed, labour and water. Planting only what you can keep watered to the end usually gives a bigger total harvest than planting more and losing it.

questions.text: You find pests on a few plants. Why should you deal with them straight away?
options: They keep feeding and multiplying, and spread to nearby plants
You should not - wait until more plants are affected so one treatment covers them all
It does not matter when you treat, as long as it is before harvest
You should not - pests usually move on by themselves within a few days
questions.explanation: Every day pests are left, they do more damage, their numbers grow and they move to neighbouring plants. A few plants are cheap and quick to treat; a whole field is not.

questions.text: Your maize leaves are drooping a little on a hot afternoon. What is the best way to decide if the field needs water?
options: Water straight away - drooping leaves always mean the soil is dry
Look at the soil surface - if the top is dry, the crop needs water
Check the soil at root depth in a few spots, e.g. squeeze a handful
Wait for the next fixed watering day, whatever the field looks like
questions.explanation: Leaves often droop in afternoon heat even when there is still water lower down, and the top few centimetres always dry out first. Soil from about a hand's length down that holds together when squeezed still has water in it. Checking first stops you wasting water - in the game, scouting a tile does this job.

questions.text: What happens when you pour much more water on a plant than the soil can hold?
options: The crop grows faster, in proportion to the extra water
The extra drains below the roots and is wasted
The soil stores the extra for the next dry week
Nothing bad - the plant takes what it needs and the rest does no harm
questions.explanation: Soil can only hold a certain amount of water. The rest drains below the roots, where the crop cannot reach it, and can carry fertiliser down with it. When water is limited, that is water another plant could have used.

questions.text: A patch of maize went without water for a long time and looks weak. It is then watered well for the rest of the season. What should you expect?
options: It catches up fully with the rest of the field
It improves, but still yields less than the rest of the field
It yields more than the rest, because it now gets extra water
It is already lost, so watering it is a waste
questions.explanation: Damage from a long dry spell is not fully undone by watering later, so that patch yields less. It is usually still worth saving unless the plants have died - but preventing the stress in the first place is worth much more than rescuing the crop afterwards.

questions.text: Your water tank is nearly empty and much of the field still needs water. What usually saves the most harvest?
options: Give the remaining water to part of the field so those plants stay healthy
Share the water equally so every plant gets a little
Give the water to the plants that already look the worst
Stop watering and keep the water in case things get worse
questions.explanation: A little water for every plant can leave the whole field stressed, so nothing yields well. Keeping a smaller part properly watered gives a real harvest from that part. The plants that look worst are often already badly damaged and give the least back for the water.

questions.text: Why is the soil loosened (tilled) before planting?
options: Mainly to add nutrients to the soil
To dry the soil out so the seed does not rot
It is only needed for weeds - seed grows just as well in hard ground
So seed touches moist soil, roots can push down, and rain soaks in
questions.explanation: Loose soil gives the seed good contact with moist soil, lets young roots grow down easily, and lets rain soak in instead of running off. Tilling does not add nutrients - that needs manure, compost or fertiliser. Don't overdo it either: soil worked into a fine powder crusts over and washes away more easily.

questions.text: What is the best way to find pests early, before they do much damage?
options: Look for damaged plants from the edge of the field
Spray the whole field every week, whether pests are there or not
Walk through the whole field often and check plants closely, under leaves too
Check only the plants near the path, since pests arrive from there
questions.explanation: Pests often start in one patch, hidden under leaves or in the growing tip, so they are easy to miss from the edge. Walking a zigzag through the field every few days and checking several plants up close finds them while only a few plants are affected. Spraying on a schedule costs money and also kills the insects that eat pests.
